title: Adab of the road
hook: the companions want to keep sitting by the road, so they're told what the road is owed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of knowledge, and your line: learn, then do. Today, out the front door and onto the street.

Do roads have rights? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says they do. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told his companions to avoid sitting along the roads. They pushed back. Those are our meeting places, they said. That's where we talk. So he didn't argue. He said, in paraphrase: if you must sit there, then give the road its right. And they asked the obvious next question. What is the road's right?
screen: `DO ROADS HAVE RIGHTS?` → `WE CAN'T HELP SITTING THERE.` → `THEN GIVE THE ROAD ITS RIGHT.`

segments.voice: His answer, in paraphrase: lowering the gaze, holding back harm, returning the greeting, and urging what is good while forbidding what is wrong. A street belongs to no one in particular, and that doesn't make it a free-for-all. Everyone on it is owed something by everyone else. First, the eyes. In al-Nur, in Pickthall's translation: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest." The next verse says the same to the believing women. On a crowded street, a lowered gaze is a kind of privacy for people who can't close a door. Second, harm. Bukhari tells of a man who found a thorny branch lying across a road and moved it aside, and Allah thanked him for it and forgave him. One branch. And in Sahih Muslim, faith has many branches, the highest the declaration that there is no god but Allah, the lowest removing something harmful from the road. Even the lowest branch is still faith. Third, the greeting, from day three hundred eighty-four. Al-Nisa, Pickthall again: "When ye are greeted with a greeting, greet ye with a better than it or return it." It's owed back, and better if you can. And the last piece turns the sidewalk into a place where people look out for one another. The companions asked for permission to sit. What they got was a job.
screen: `A STREET OWES, AND IS OWED.` · `LOWER THE GAZE.` · `MOVE THE THORNY BRANCH.` · `RETURN THE GREETING, OR BETTER.`

segments.voice: Picture the street, hallway or parking lot you'll pass through next, and the people on it. Let your eyes come down gently where they don't need to wander, see your hand moving whatever's in the way, a bottle, a cart, a bag in the aisle, and hear yourself answering a greeting a little warmer than it came. If you pray, you can return a salam with wa 'alaykum al-salam.
Adab of the road. The manners of shared space: lower the gaze, hold back harm and clear it away, return the greeting, and urge the good. Today's word.
Your line: the road's rights. Even the lowest branch is still faith. See you at the market tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of the road's rights when teaching public manners, and treat lowering the gaze, returning salam and removing harm from the path as acts of faith.

original.note: Arabic: a right, a due; the road's haqq.

trapdoor: what you thought: the adab of the road is traffic manners.
what it means: shared space has a claim on everyone in it: eyes lowered, harm cleared away, greetings returned, good encouraged.
what a scholar hears: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri's hadith on the road's haqq, beside Muslim's report that removing harm from the road is a branch of faith.

chat.says: Why would moving a branch off the sidewalk count as faith?
options: A hadith calls removing harm from the road the lowest branch of faith. Still faith.
It doesn't. Faith is only belief and prayer; the street is just manners.
Only if someone sees you do it, so it sets an example for others.
chat.meaning: In Sahih Muslim, faith has many branches, the highest the declaration of no god but Allah, the lowest removing harm from the road.
